title: The summit
hook: five years of mornings: a carpenter's son, a book, a long story, many rooms, a life; the hill goes on, and so do you
tomorrow: the hill goes on. where will you start again tomorrow morning?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the message at the empty tomb, with Peter named on his own: he goes before you, into Galilee.

On a hike, the climb is all breath and feet and the next rock. Then the top, and you turn around: the whole valley at once, roads and towns and people you couldn't see on the way up. Five years of mornings are down there too. A carpenter's son from Nazareth. A book, read page by page. A long story. A house with many rooms. A life to live it in.
screen: `ALL BREATH AND FEET.` → `THEN THE TOP. TURN AROUND.` → `FIVE YEARS OF MORNINGS.`

segments.voice: So what is a summit for? A psalm answers, in the King James: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth." The help isn't the hill. The hill is where you look up from. In Mark, Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain and is transfigured before them. Peter says, "Master, it is good for us to be here," and offers to build shelters so they can stay. The story doesn't stay. A cloud, a voice, and they come down, to a crowd, an argument, and a father with a sick son. A summit is for seeing clearly, then going back down to people. And from up here you can see how many people there are. Paul, speaking in Athens, says God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." Muslims have a verse that sounds close. The Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." One family, made different so they'd know one another. That's real shared ground. The difference is real too: Paul's speech goes on to Jesus raised from the dead, and Muslims understand Jesus differently. Neither has to pretend otherwise to look out on the same valley. The psalm ends past the top: "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore." Not a finish line. A place to begin again.
screen: `THE HILL IS WHERE YOU LOOK UP.` · `GOOD TO BE HERE, THEN DOWN.` · `ONE BLOOD, ALL NATIONS.` · `GOING OUT AND COMING IN.` · then, large: `START AGAIN, FROM HERE.`

segments.voice: Stand, if you can, and be still. Look out at whatever is in front of you, a window, a wall, a patch of sky, and let five years of mornings come back: a face, a line, a day that stayed. Then give thanks for one of them, out loud.
The summit. A place to stand still and look back, and then, like Peter, James and John, to come down again among people.
Your line: start again, from here. The hill goes on, and so do you, wherever the road leads next.

howItsDone: Churches remember the transfiguration on the mountain in the church year, and some Christians read or sing Psalm 121 before a journey or a parting.

fork.setup: you're Peter on the mountain. it's good to be here, and you offer to build shelters and stay. what happens next in Mark?
options: they stay up there for days.
a cloud, a voice, and they come down to a waiting crowd.
fork.reveal: Mark 9:7–17: the cloud, the voice, the coming down, and at the bottom a crowd, scribes questioning, and a father with his son. the summit is for seeing, then going back to people.

original.note: Greek: he was transfigured, changed in form, in Mark 9:2.

what a scholar hears: Psalm 121 is headed a song of degrees, and ends on going out and coming in, a journey, not an arrival.

chat.says: train to chicago, car full of strangers, like five languages. pop always says "one blood." where's that from?
options: Acts 17: Paul says God 'hath made of one blood all nations of men.' Everyone in that car.
It's a family saying about being related to Pop, not anything from the Bible.
It means Christians only: one blood is the people who share communion together.
chat.meaning: In Athens, Paul says God made of one blood all nations of men. The Qur'an has a verse that sounds close: nations and tribes, made to know one another.

Nazareth.meaning: the town in Galilee where Jesus grew up

Athens.meaning: the Greek city where Paul gave a speech

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (shape: wisdom: what is a summit for? Psalm 121, the transfiguration and coming down, and the unity thread). Title, word, carry and sources kept; Acts 17:26 and Qur'an 49:13 added.

Unity thread (weekly neighbor): Islam. Qur'an 49:13 quoted from Pickthall (1930); please verify the exact wording against the Pickthall text. Shared ground: one human family made into nations to know one another (Acts 17:26 / Qur'an 49:13). Honest difference: Paul's speech goes on to Jesus raised from the dead (Acts 17:31), and Muslims understand Jesus differently. No ranking, and nothing says the traditions are the same. The Prophet Muhammad is not named, so no honorific is needed; please have a Muslim reviewer confirm the framing is fair.
